snippet.title: Mount Etna's New Cone: Chris Horsley Grabs a Red Hot Lava Bomb
snippet.description:
Chris Horsley scales erupting Mount Etna to map a newborn cone and seize a fresh lava bomb for INGV, battling brutal winds, ash, and rockfall to deliver life-saving data.

On Exploration Volcano, we join Chris and a small crew in Sicily as Etna enters a new eruptive stage. Guided by local experts and INGV scientists, the team targets the southeast crater where a new cone has risen within maybe 20 metres of the volcano's highest point. Inside the 24/7 surveillance room, Boris explains how infrasound and seismic signals locate ongoing explosions and help keep Catania's airspace and residents safe.

The ascent is brutal: a cable car, then a 14-ton Unimog to 2,900 m, and finally a lung-busting climb in -25 C wind chill over 2017 lava flows and the rim of the vast Valle del Bove. With heavy packs of drones, thermal cameras, and batteries, the crew battles volcanic sand, gas clouds, and constant rockfall.

At the rim, violent bursts send incandescent bombs arcing above the crater. Chris launches a drone to build a 3D map of the new cone, but fierce winds and freezing temps drain the batteries fast, forcing a partial survey. With time running out, the mission shifts to securing a fresh sample.

Dodging the fall zone, Chris and volcanologist Carmelo sprint in to grab a still-glowing lava bomb using welding gloves. A quick surface reading hits about 480 C before the team quenches it with water. Back in town, the sample goes to Boris at INGV to compare with previous rocks. More crystals could indicate older, degassed magma in the conduit; less crystalline, more primitive magma often signals gas-rich, potentially more explosive activity.

In 2021 Etna unleashed more than 50 violent eruptions, with kilometer-high lava fountains, ash blanketing nearby towns, and red-hot flows that helped raise a new summit to 3,357 m. Mapping and sampling like this feed the multi-parameter monitoring that helps scientists anticipate changes and protect the people living on Etna's slopes.
